answer: Data literacy is the ability to read, understand, work with, and communicate data [1][2]. It is not limited to statistics or programming, but rather encompasses the ability to recognise what a dataset or indicator is showing, interpret data, and explain key findings to others [2]. Data literacy is essential for public health professionals to make informed decisions based on data [2]. It involves being able to ask questions about data production and reliability [2].

The key dimensions of data quality are Accuracy, Completeness, Timeliness, and Validity. [1][2] 

These dimensions provide a simple checklist for judging whether data are ready to be used. [1][2] 

They are essential for ensuring that data can be trusted to reflect reality and support sound conclusions. [1][2]

Data wrangling is the process of transforming raw, messy data into an analysis-ready dataset. It includes all the practical work that sits between receiving a file and being able to use it to answer a question. [1][2]

Line charts are the main tool for showing how an indicator changes over time. They rely on temporal data on the horizontal axis and numerical data on the vertical axis. Values at regular time points (days, weeks, months) are plotted and then connected by a line. [1][2]

Logistic regression is used for binary outcomes, predicting whether an event (e.g. getting sick) is likely to happen [1][3]. Poisson regression is used for count outcomes, predicting how often events (e.g. disease cases) occur over time or across places [1][3]. This difference in outcome type is the key distinction between the two models [1][3].

La régression logistique est utilisée pour prédire si un événement (par exemple, contracter une maladie) est susceptible de se produire, tandis que la régression de Poisson est utilisée pour prédire la fréquence d'un événement (par exemple, le nombre de cas de maladie) sur une période de temps ou dans une zone spécifique.
